lessons.title: Particles and ions
points: Z = protons. A = protons + neutrons. Neutrons = A - Z. Charge = protons - electrons. In a neutral atom, electrons = protons.

Protons: +1, nucleus. Neutrons: 0, nucleus. Electrons: -1, outside nucleus, much lighter. Example: 17 p, 18 n, 18 e gives Z=17, A=35, charge -1. Changing electrons makes an ion; changing protons changes the element.

lessons.title: Isotopes and averages
points: Isotopes: same proton number, different neutron numbers. Average atomic mass = sum of (isotope mass x abundance/100).

Example: 35 u at 75% and 37 u at 25% gives 35(0.75)+37(0.25)=35.5 u. Check the answer lies between the isotope masses and nearer the more abundant isotope. Atomic mass unit: 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

lessons.title: Models and electron shells
points: Dalton: solid-sphere model. Thomson: electron, plum-pudding model. Rutherford: small dense positive nucleus, mostly empty space. Bohr: definite energy levels. Chadwick: neutron.

Most alpha particles passed through gold foil; a few deflected strongly. That supports Rutherford's conclusions. First-20-element shell examples: Al 2,8,3; S 2,8,6; Cl 2,8,7; K 2,8,8,1; Ca 2,8,8,2. Light is emitted when excited electrons fall to lower levels.

lessons.title: Periodic table and families
points: Modern table: increasing atomic number. Mendeleev used atomic mass and left gaps. Group = vertical column; period = horizontal row. Main-group family similarities come from similar valence electrons.

Group 1 alkali metals: 1 valence electron. Group 2 alkaline earths: 2. Group 17 halogens: 7. Group 18 noble gases: full shell; helium has 2. Metals conduct and are usually lustrous; metalloids have mixed properties; non-metals usually conduct poorly.

lessons.title: Trends: explain the reason
points: Atomic radius increases DOWN a group (more shells and shielding), decreases ACROSS a period (greater nuclear attraction in the same shell). Ionization energy and electronegativity generally follow the opposite pattern.

First ionization energy: energy to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom. Electron affinity: energy change when a gaseous neutral atom gains an electron; many exceptions occur. Cations are smaller than their atoms; anions are larger. F < Cl < Br < I in radius; Li < Na < K < Rb.

lessons.title: Ion charges and the zero-sum rule
points: Cations lose electrons and become positive. Anions gain electrons and become negative. Typical charges: groups 1 +1, 2 +2, 13 +3, 15 -3, 16 -2, 17 -1. The octet rule is a useful model with exceptions; H needs 2 electrons.
Total charge must be zero in an ionic formula. Al3+ and O2-: 2(+3)+3(-2)=0, so Al2O3. Mg2+ and PO4^3-: Mg3(PO4)2. Reduce ratios: Ca2+ and O2- give CaO, not Ca2O2.

lessons.title: Polyatomic ions to memorize
points: NH4+ ammonium; OH- hydroxide; NO3- nitrate; NO2- nitrite; SO4^2- sulfate; SO3^2- sulfite; CO3^2- carbonate; HCO3- hydrogen carbonate.

PO4^3- phosphate; HPO4^2- hydrogen phosphate; ClO- hypochlorite; ClO3- chlorate; ClO4- perchlorate; CN- cyanide; BrO3- bromate. Keep a polyatomic ion together: Al(NO3)3, (NH4)3PO4. Parentheses mean more than one whole ion.

lessons.title: Naming ionic compounds
points: Name the cation first, then the anion. Monatomic anions end in -ide. Keep polyatomic-ion names. A Roman numeral gives the variable-charge metal's charge, not the atom count.

FeCl3: iron(III) chloride. FeS: iron(II) sulfide. Mg(ClO3)2: magnesium chlorate. PbO2: lead(IV) oxide. CuCl: copper(I) chloride. Na2SO4: sodium sulfate. IUPAC standard names help scientists communicate chemical identities clearly.

lessons.title: Molecular names and hydrates
points: Prefixes: mono 1, di 2, tri 3, tetra 4, penta 5, hexa 6, hepta 7, octa 8, nona 9, deca 10. Usually omit mono on the first element. The second ends in -ide.

PCl5 phosphorus pentachloride; N2O5 dinitrogen pentoxide; CF4 carbon tetrafluoride; SO2 sulfur dioxide; NO nitrogen monoxide; S2Cl2 disulfur dichloride. CoCl2.6H2O: cobalt(II) chloride hexahydrate. Anhydrous CoCl2 has no water of crystallization.

lessons.title: Bonding and conductivity
points: Ionic bonding: electrostatic attraction between opposite ions. Electron transfer produces ions. Covalent bonding: sharing electron pairs. Ionic substances form lattices; simple molecular substances contain separate molecules.

Ionic solids: usually high melting, hard and brittle. Solid ions cannot move, so do not conduct. Molten or dissolved ions can move and conduct. Simple molecular substances usually have lower melting/boiling points and poor conductivity. Test melting point, molten conductivity and solution conductivity; solubility alone is not decisive.

lessons.title: Electronegativity and polarity
points: Electronegativity is the ability of a bonded atom to attract shared electrons. Difference = larger EN minus smaller EN. Higher EN atom is partially negative. Larger difference means a more polar bond.

Your PPT rule: 0 non-polar; between 0 and 1.7 polar; 1.7 or above predicts ionic. This is a guide: HF is polar covalent and CaS ionic despite borderline values. Your PPT labels C-H (0.4) weakly polar. Use the question's table and requested convention. H-F > H-Cl; O-H > C-H; C-N > N-N in polarity.

lessons.title: Lewis structures: count first
points: Total valence electrons: add atomic contributions; ADD electrons for negative charge, SUBTRACT for positive. Draw bonds, complete outer atoms, place remaining electrons, form multiple bonds if needed, then check totals and charges.

One bond = 2 electrons; double = 4; triple = 6. H2O: 8 total, 2 bonds, 2 lone pairs on O. NH3: 8 total, 3 bonds, 1 lone pair on N. CH4: 8 total, 4 bonds, no lone pair on C. Structural formulas omit lone-pair dots; Lewis structures include them.

lessons.title: Lewis structures: homework targets
points: I2: I-I, 3 lone pairs per I. CF4: 4 C-F bonds, 3 lone pairs per F. H2S: 2 S-H bonds, 2 lone pairs on S. PCl3 and NF3: 3 bonds and 1 lone pair on central atom; each halogen has 3 lone pairs.

C2H2: H-C triple-bond C-H; no carbon lone pairs. Ethanol: CH3-CH2-OH; ether: CH3-O-CH3; each O has 2 lone pairs. SO2 has resonance; one expanded-octet drawing has two S=O bonds and one S lone pair. CsCl is ionic: Cs+ and Cl-, not a covalent molecule.

lessons.title: Charged Lewis structures
points: H3O+: 8 electrons, 3 O-H bonds, 1 lone pair on O. ClO-: 14 electrons, Cl-O single bond, 3 lone pairs on each atom. HCO3-: 24 electrons, HO-C(=O)-O-, 2 equivalent contributors.

CO3^2-: 24 electrons; one C=O and two C-O- in each contributor; 3 equivalent contributors. NO3-: 24 electrons; N has +1 formal charge, two singly bonded O have -1 each. Put ions in brackets with the overall charge. Resonance contributors are models of delocalized bonding, not molecules switching back and forth.

lessons.title: Radiation and practical chemistry
points: Radioisotopes have unstable nuclei that decay and emit radiation. Alpha: helium nucleus, +2, stopped by paper. Beta-minus: electron, -1, reduced by aluminium. Gamma: electromagnetic radiation, neutral, strongly penetrating; thick lead or concrete attenuates it.

Uses in lessons: Am-241 smoke detectors; Co-60 food irradiation; C-14 dating once-living material; I-131 thyroid treatment; Tc-99m medical imaging. Flame tests: Li crimson, Na yellow, K lilac, Ca orange-red, Sr red, Cu blue-green. Colour comes from electrons releasing energy as light.

lessons.title: Nature of chemistry and applications
points: Matter has mass and occupies space. Chemistry studies matter, its properties and changes. Empirical knowledge comes from observation; theoretical knowledge uses explanations/models. Macroscopic means observable scale; microscopic means particles.

Science explains; technology applies. Green chemistry reduces hazardous substances, waste and energy use. IUPAC: International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry. Sugar and sweeteners differ in structure and properties: compare taste, energy contribution, stability, cost and evidence-based suitability. Molecular shape matters as well as bond polarity.

questions.q: What does atomic number Z count?
questions.why: An element is identified by its proton number.

questions.q: A neutral atom has 19 protons. How many electrons?
questions.why: Neutral means equal positive and negative charges.

questions.q: Isotopes of one element differ in...
questions.why: Same protons, different neutrons.
Cathode-ray experiments supported Thomson's electron discovery.
Most passed through; a few were strongly deflected.

questions.q: Who proposed definite electron energy levels?
questions.why: Bohr linked allowed energy levels to line spectra.
13 electrons: 2 in first, 8 in second, 3 in third.

questions.q: An atom gains one electron. What changes?
questions.why: Ordinary ion formation changes electrons, not the nucleus.
Mendeleev used mass; modern ordering uses atomic number.
Period = horizontal row.

questions.q: Which family has seven valence electrons?
questions.why: Group 17 has seven valence electrons.
Radius grows down Group 17 as shells are added.
Ca is below Mg in Group 2, with an extra shell.

questions.q: Which is larger: Na or Na+?
questions.why: Na+ loses its outer shell and becomes smaller.
Increasing nuclear attraction pulls same-shell electrons closer.

questions.q: First ionization energy down a group generally...
questions.why: More distance and shielding make the outer electron easier to remove.

options: Energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron
questions.why: Do not confuse gaining an electron with ionization energy (removing one).

questions.q: Highest electronegativity among F, Cl, Br and I?
questions.why: Fluorine is highest in your course scale.
Transfer forms ions; electrostatic attraction is the bond.
Single: one pair; double: two; triple: three.

questions.q: Why does solid NaCl not conduct?
questions.why: Molten NaCl conducts because the ions become mobile.

options: Shifting layers brings like charges together
There are no forces between ions
questions.why: Like charges repel and the crystal fractures.

options: Low melting points and poor conductivity
questions.why: These are general tendencies, not universal for all covalent substances.
The formula gives the simplest ion ratio in the lattice.
Use absolute difference: 3.4 - 2.6 = 0.8.
F attracts bonding electrons more strongly than Cl.
Identical atoms have equal electronegativity.
Shared electrons are attracted toward it.
3 Mg2+ balance 2 phosphate ions of charge 3-.
Three nitrate ions balance one Al3+.
Three ammonium +1 ions balance phosphate -3.
Sulfide is S2-; sulfate is SO4^2-.
ClO3- is chlorate; Cl- is chloride.
Five chlorine atoms require penta-.
Tetra means four.
Di = 2 nitrogen, penta = 5 oxygen; pentoxide spelling.

questions.q: A Roman numeral in iron(III) means...
questions.why: Roman numeral gives the metal ion charge.
One Cl- needs Cu+.
Sn4+ needs two O2- ions.
Six water molecules per formula unit of the hydrate.
Nitrate has three O; nitrite has two.

questions.q: Water: how many lone pairs on oxygen?
questions.why: 8 electrons total: 4 in bonds, 4 in two lone pairs.

questions.q: Ammonia: bonds and lone pairs on N?
questions.why: N supplies five valence electrons; three H add three.

questions.q: A triple bond contains how many electrons?
questions.why: Three shared pairs = six electrons.

questions.q: What must a Lewis structure show beyond a structural formula?
questions.why: Include all valence electrons and ion charges where needed.
H-C triple-bond C-H gives each carbon an octet.
Cs is a metal forming Cs+; Cl forms Cl-.

questions.q: Carbonate has how many equivalent resonance contributors?
questions.why: Place C=O at each oxygen in turn; actual bonding is delocalized.

questions.q: Which radiation is a helium nucleus?
questions.why: Alpha contains two protons and two neutrons.

questions.q: Which radiation has no mass or electric charge?
questions.why: Gamma is electromagnetic radiation.
Potassium is lilac; copper blue-green; lithium crimson.
